VAMPI penetration testing report 

Prepared by: obonguko, mfoniso ubon 

ID: CSF/API/25B/1056 

Target application: VAMPI 

Testing window: 17-23 November 

Executive summary: 

APIs form the present-day bridges that allow software systems to communicate with each other, share data, and perform actions seamlessly. Today, over 80% of web applications rely on APIs to fetch data, enable user interaction, integrate services, and deliver dynamic real-time functionality. With great power comes great responsibility— Lots of security breaches have happened in major organizations like LinkedIn in 2021, which impacted over 700 million users, and T-Mobile (2023), which affected 40 million users, was caused by API vulnerabilities. Seeing the important role and impact APIs have in modern web applications, it is important for us as security personnel to be able to identify vulnerabilities associated with Application Programming Interfaces, how the vulnerabilities can be spotted, and how to mitigate each vulnerability. In this lab, I carried out a penetration test on a vulnerable API, VAmPI, identifying vulnerabilities like broken object-level authentication, Broken Authentication, Broken object property-level authorization, and recommending solutions for the vulnerabilities found. 

**Methodology:** 

This testing used a gray box technique 

**Tools used** 

Burp Suite (intercepting and testing) 

APIscanner (scan for endpoints) 

VSCODE ( yaml file inspection) 

Postman (manual api testing) 

**Process overview:** 

● Converted the Swagger file to JSON 

● Turned on the proxy for Burp Suite and Postman 

● Imported the file to Postman 

Key findings 

**Broken Object-level Authorization** 

Broken Object-Level Authorization, often called BOLA, is one of the most dangerous weaknesses found in modern APIs. APIs act as the highways that shuttle sensitive data between systems, users, and services, and when authorization checks are weak, those highways can easily turn into unrestricted access roads. BOLA happens when an API does not  
properly verify whether the person making a request actually owns the data they are trying to access. An attacker can simply change an ID in the request, such as a user ID or name, and suddenly retrieve information that belongs to someone else. This flaw has been responsible for several large-scale data breaches because it gives attackers a direct line into private user information with very little effort. 

In these screenshots below, I’ve simply demonstrated how broken object-level authentication can be exploited 

![][image1]Changing the user's password and sending it to Burp  
![][image2]Forwarding the request to the server using Burp 

![][image3]The response code shows that the vulnerability has been exploited successfully  
![][image4]To prevent BOLA, always check if the user requesting access to an object has the necessary permissions for that specific object and action. 

**Broken object property level authorization (BOPLA)** 

This vulnerability occurs when an API endpoint successfully implements checks for object-level access (i.e., verifying the user can access the entire resource) but fails to enforce authorization checks at the individual property level within that resource.  
![][image5]i added the object admin and the property true, which came back with the status code 200![][image6]  
To prevent BOPLA, never trust input data from the client side, and Properties that should never be updated by the user (like user\_role, account\_balance, or isAdmin) must be excluded from any update process. Enforcing strict access controls will prevent Bopla 

**Security misconfiguration** 

This arises from errors, oversights, or an inherent lack of hardening in the configuration of the API’s components, leaving systems in their insecure default state or enabling unnecessary features, which could lead to exploitations 

In this screenshot, the debug mode was able to retrieve all the data relating to users on this system. It included their usernames, passwords, emails, etc. 

![][image7]To prevent this vulnerability, maintain secure configuration baselines throughout the environment, limit information disclosure, use TLS/SSL, and manage CORS policies strictly.
